newsitem.title: UK: UK voters back more spending on health - Heseltine.
newsitem.headline: UK voters back more spending on health - Heseltine.

text.p: Britain's deputy prime minister, Michael Heseltine, said on Friday the government planned to spend more on the National Health Service (NHS) and that voters would back that policy, even in preference to tax cuts. Prime Minister John Major is set to end the Conservatives' annual conference today with a pledge to increase spending in real terms on the NHS, and Heseltine told BBC radio this was "the first priority when we look at public expenditure rounds".

Asked whether some voters might prefer that extra money to be given back, in the form of tax cuts, Heseltine said: "I don't think so, when it comes to health." He said the Conservative government had made health spending the priority even during the recession when it had been necessary to raise taxes to increase spending on the NHS.
In contrast, the Labour Party always wanted to put up taxes and extend the state "instinctively", he said. "It's no good trying to pretend that their tax-hungry attitudes have changed."

Heseltine said confidence was returning to the retail and housing markets, and he reaffirmed the government's intention to hold the next general election later rather than sooner. "We were elected for five years," he said.
The last possible month for the election is May 1997.
